config.prompt: Pair each ratio with its definition:
config.why: The real content is that they are functions of angle alone — scale the triangle and the ratios never move.

config.prompt: A '55-inch' 16:9 TV has width ≈ 47.9 inches. Roughly how wide is it?
config.why: √((16k)² + (9k)²) = k·√337 ≈ 18.36k = 55, so k ≈ 3.0 — one theorem converts the diagonal on the price tag into whether the screen fits your shelf.

config.prompt: One of these claims about Pythagoras is wrong — click it:
lines: a² + b² = c² is exactly the right-angle condition.
The size of the failure is what the cosine rule measures.
a² + b² = c² applies to any triangle.
config.correction: a² + b² = c² holds exactly for right angles — for non-right triangles it fails, and the cosine rule supplies the correction term.
config.why: The hypotenuse is always the longest side, opposite the right angle — checking this catches swapped-label errors before they happen.

activities.anchor: a 6 m ladder leans against a wall at 70°
activities.caption: call the ladder's reach
activities.name: trigLadderEst

config.prompt: A 6 m ladder leans against a wall at 70° to the ground. Roughly how high does it reach?
config.why: 6 × sin 70° ≈ 6 × 0.940 = 5.64 m — and the foot sits 6 × cos 70° ≈ 2.05 m from the wall.
config.context: to reach a window 5 m up, the required angle is sin⁻¹(5/6) ≈ 56.4°

activities.anchor: Three special angles come from half-squares
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the exact values
activities.name: trigExactCloze

config.text: The exact values worth knowing cold: 45° (half a square): sin = cos = %%0%%. 60° (half an equilateral triangle): sin = %%1%%/2. 30° (the same triangle from the other corner): sin = %%2%%.
config.hint: One surd from the square's diagonal, one from the equilateral triangle, and one plain half.

activities.caption: bet before you read on — the complementary swap
activities.name: trigCompPredict

config.q: Why is sin θ = cos(90° − θ) always true?
choices: Complementary angles swap the roles of opposite and adjacent
Sine and cosine are the same function
config.why: In the other acute corner of the same triangle, the opposite and adjacent sides exchange — which is the same fact the graph shows as a quarter-period shift.

activities.anchor: the most-used fact in the subject
activities.caption: the identity at work
activities.name: trigIdBranch

config.root: sin θ = 0.6 for an angle in the first quadrant. What is cos θ?

choices.label: 0.8 — from sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
choices.feedback: Right: cos²θ = 1 − 0.36 = 0.64, so cos θ = 0.8 — the circle's equation x² + y² = 1 in trig clothing.

choices.label: 0.4 — they must add to 1
choices.feedback: They add to 1 only after squaring: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, not sin θ + cos θ = 1.

choices.label: Cannot tell without the angle
choices.feedback: You can: the identity pins cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ, and the quadrant fixes the sign.

right.text: Given sin θ, find cos θ — the source of every such manipulation.

add.text: The squares add to 1; the functions themselves do not.

tell.text: The identity plus the quadrant is all the information needed.

config.why: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 is the unit circle's equation — the most-used fact in the subject.

activities.anchor: the sine rule works with any side paired with any angle
activities.caption: find the pairing error
activities.name: trigSineSpot

config.prompt: One of these claims about the sine rule is wrong — click it:
lines: The sine rule: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C.
It relates each side to the angle opposite it.
The cosine rule is Pythagoras with a correction term for non-right angles.
The sine rule works with any side paired with any angle.
config.correction: It only relates a side to the angle opposite it — mismatching the pairs is the most common source of wrong answers in this topic.
config.why: a is the side facing A, and so on — the pairing is the rule.
